articles.title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
articles.excerpt: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake. More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday. While the official death toll remains at 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing. He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses. Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed. In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort. On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed. Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped.In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed.

articles.title: Trump says he switched planes after Nato summit because of possible threat
articles.excerpt: Technically "Air Force One" is the call sign for any aircraft carrying the US president. But on this occasion, the C-32A used the call sign "Reach 18", while the aircraft carrying the journalists continued to use "AF1" in order to keep up the ruse.Remaining on the original aircraft were members of Trump's cabinet, according to the New York Times. The outlet, citing two anonymous officials, reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were on board.Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet.The president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington.During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap.Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said at the time: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with."He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list".Jose Zamora, regional director for the Americas for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said in a statement that the Trump administration "has a responsibility to ensure that journalists covering the president are not unnecessarily exposed to danger"."Reporters should be informed of credible security threats so they can make informed decisions about their safety," he added.

articles.title: Trump's dramatic plane swap hints at personal stakes of Iran war
articles.excerpt: "I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonathan Karl, in a phone conversation the day after he launched the US military campaign against Iran in February.An Israeli airstrike, conducted with US approval and co-ordination, had just killed the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian leaders – and Trump drew a direct line from that attack to threats and alleged plots the Iranians had made against him in previous years.Trump has refrained from similar remarks in the ensuing six months of warfare, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed the view."Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh," he said in March, noting that an unnamed Iranian who he said led an assassination unit had been killed in US strikes.These comments hint at the personal nature of this war – and the concerns by the president and his security team of the threat Iran still poses to his safety.Those concerns were dramatically illustrated by this week's revelation that Trump secretly switched to an alternate aircraft on his flight back from the Nato summit in Turkey last month. He left the media and most of the White House staff to depart on the presidential Air Force One 747 jet, which became, essentially, a decoy.It was an elaborate ruse, which included the president being transported to and from aircraft inside a catering truck, in response to what American officials reportedly believed to be credible intelligence of an Iranian missile threat to Air Force One.The White House has given little detail about this threat - but nonetheless it marks another striking episode in the turbulent history of Trump's relationship with Iran.Government security experts have said such measures are not unusual when a president travels in or near a warzone.

articles.title: US says helicopter fired missiles to disable ship breaking Iran blockade
articles.excerpt: The US military says one of its helicopters has fired missiles to disable "the steering gear" of a cargo ship attempting to violate the US blockade of Iranian ports.In a statement, US Central Command (Centcom) says its MH-60 aircraft on Tuesday fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Panama-flagged M/V Vela Nova vessel, as it attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman.Centcom said it acted after "the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces". The vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran", it added.Iran has not commented. The US has been enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports, following failed attempts to end the war it and Israel started on 28 February. Tehran retaliated by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states across the Gulf. It has also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - a key oil shipping waterway.A fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the strait before the war and prices have fluctuated wildly since then.Mediators have so far failed to bring the sides to an agreement on reopening the strait - and, since the latest ceasefire collapsed in June, both the US and Iran have exchanged fire intermittently. In its statement on X, Centcom said M/V Vela attempted to sail to an Iranian port without naming it. It also did not say whether there were any casualties or injuries.It says the US blockade "remains in full effect", adding that as of 11 August Centcom has "redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to run the blockade, disabled 3 non-compliant vessels, and boarded 2".In a separate development on Tuesday, Yemen's internationally recognised government said six people were killed and 10 injured in strikes by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they hit a vessel carrying Saudi military equipment. It appears to be the first deadly attack by the group on a ship since the war began.

articles.title: Baby Shark Boy set to make K-pop debut
articles.excerpt: At just seven years old, Park Geon-roung starred in the Baby Shark music video that went on to become the most-watched YouTube clip of all time, with 17 billion views - and counting. Now, Baby Shark Boy wants to be a K-pop star. He's backed by Pinkfong, the South Korean kids entertainment company that made Baby Shark - but will they find success again? The BBC's Tessa Wong explains everything you need to know about his upcoming debut.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez
articles.excerpt: The couple have been together for 10 years, after they met at a Gucci shop in Madrid where Rodríguez was working. He was playing at the Spanish club Real Madrid at the time.They announced their engagement on 11 August last year. At the time, Rodríguez posted a picture of a large ring, writing "Yes I do. In this and in all my lives" in her native Spanish.Ronaldo has scored nearly 1,000 goals in a career in which he has played for Lisbon-based Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia and Portugal.He recently played in his sixth World Cup, a record for appearances in the men's finals which he shares with Lionel Messi of Argentina.

articles.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
articles.excerpt: Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment.A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it.The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure.Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row.Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced.Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity.The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law."We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC.As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon."We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said.Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions.

articles.title: Bondi Beach shooting hero's assault charges dropped by police
articles.excerpt: A man who was hailed a hero for disarming one of the Bondi Beach shooters in December has had assault charges against him dropped by police.Ahmed al Ahmed was charged in June with domestic violence common assault, as well as stalking and intimidation, after an alleged incident with his father in March at a home in southwest Sydney. Ahmed denied both charges.On Wednesday, in a local Sydney court, prosecutors withdrew the charges after it was agreed that Ahmed would abide by an apprehended domestic violence order for 12 months, limiting his contact with his father.Outside the court, Ahmed, 44, welcomed the development, telling reporters that he was a "free man" and that he hoped for "peace".Defence lawyer Mohamed Sakr said in court that the order prohibiting Ahmed from assaulting, threatening, stalking or intimidating his father had been accepted without admissions, according to national broadcaster ABC.Ahmed made global headlines last year after footage emerged of him tackling one of two gunmen who had opened fire during a Jewish event at Sydney's Bondi Beach, killing 15 people.

articles.title: New Zealand PM survives second leadership challenge ahead of election
articles.excerpt: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a vote of confidence before a general election due in November, saying he has the "full support" of his ruling National Party.Luxon had called for an "urgent" meeting with his National Party caucus on Wednesday to address "‌increased speculation about [his] leadership"."I have the full support of our caucus... Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he told reporters after the meeting which lasted more than three hours.This was the second challenge to his leadership in four months. Support for Luxon and his party remained weak amid sluggish economic growth and a series of missteps by the leader.Last week, Luxon drew backlash after suggesting a possible referendum on the country's electoral system on live radio, without prior consultation with his party colleagues.Earlier this month, the 56-year-old riled up New Zealand's business community after a speech calling on small business owners to "be adult". He said the country's businesses had a "parent-child mentality" with the central government and relied too often on handouts.He later apologised and acknowledged many were going through tough times.The former Air New Zealand boss led his centre-right party to victory in the 2023 elections vowing to bring down the cost of living and reduce taxes."My pledge to you is that our government will deliver for every New Zealander," he said then.But his party has suffered in opinion polls in recent months as the economy continues to stall, with unemployment rising to an 11-year high of 5.6%.A 1News Verian poll published on Wednesday morning showed Luxon's preferred prime minister rating slide to 17% – a new low for his time in office – but he remains ahead of all other candidates included in the poll.New Zealand will hold its next general election on 7 November.

articles.title: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
articles.excerpt: France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry.From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions.Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing. "It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement."This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine Stévenin added.She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer.""This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said.But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market.One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin.

articles.title: Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president
articles.excerpt: Hungary's parliament has elected András Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state. The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous. His task will be to monitor Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace Orbán's constitution of 2011."We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," András Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6. "The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs."All 51 MPs belonging to Orbán's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, Tamás Sulyok, from the post last month. In his speech, András Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution. Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking Orbán's legacy. Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution. The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which Orbán used to govern by decree, were all cancelled. The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government. Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny".

articles.title: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.excerpt: Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally.In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks.The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border.In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea"."The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world.He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments. It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea.Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces.

articles.title: Luigi Mangione murder trial to have anonymous jury
articles.excerpt: The jury in the New York state trial of Luigi Mangione will remain anonymous, the judge overseeing the case ruled on Tuesday.Mangione has pleaded not guilty to the killing of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel in December 2024. The case has been at the centre of an online frenzy between Mangione's backers - many of whom see the 28-year-old as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics, who analyse his intentions and possible political views. In Tuesday's hearing, Judge Gregory Carro decided the 12-person jury would be anonymous to the public because of the intense spotlight on the case.Mangione attended the final pre-trial hearing dressed in a charcoal grey suit with his hair clipped short. He sat silently at the defence table while his attorneys conferred with the judge. The trial begins next month, with jury selection scheduled to start on 8 September.Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences. He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty.Here's what to know about the upcoming trial, and what questions remain.

articles.title: Ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
articles.excerpt: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to the Russian capital, Moscow, with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power.Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence.Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule.In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces.That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year.Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death".The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher.

articles.title: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health
articles.excerpt: President Donald Trump said a former US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released."After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place.Robert Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested in 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state.Gilman was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration.The BBC understands Gilman is expected to arrive early on Wednesday morning at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated.Trump said he spoke to Gilman on the phone, "and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" "During my Administration, we have prioritised bringing home Americans detained abroad, and have done so at a level never seen before," Trump added.Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer for Global Reach, the advocacy group representing the former Marine, told Reuters that Gilman was released because the Russian government realised "they're not losing any geopolitical power position by releasing him. This is a humanitarian release".Gilman served in the US Marines for a year until August 2020.He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years.He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check.

articles.title: Thailand suspends new gun permits after mass shooting
articles.excerpt: Thailand's government will immediately stop issuing gun permits after a shooting incident last week in which a 14-year-old killed eight people and himself.Existing gun owners are already banned from carrying their weapons in public.The South East Asian country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in the region, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, and high levels of gun crime.In response to the recent shooting, the prime minister has promised to pass tough new gun control laws with severe penalties, suspending new permits in the meantime.Last Friday, a pupil at Debsirin Nonthaburi School outside Bangkok shot his grandparents using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before opening fire at teachers and students at school, authorities say.Both grandparents, five staff members at the school and one 12-year-old girl died. Police believe the shooter may have taught himself to use a gun via social media.They say there is evidence that the boy watched violent content online, and that he showed a strong interest in learning how to handle guns.His consumption of this content as well as anxiety over studies and family issues might have also fuelled his actions, they add.

articles.title: Canada flight cancelled after child refuses to wear seat belt
articles.excerpt: The cancellation of a flight in Canada after a child refused to wear a seat belt has reignited a debate about the etiquette and safety procedures relating to children travelling on planes.The Porter Airlines flight, which was preparing to depart from Victoria to Toronto on 6 August had to return to the terminal as a "young child was standing in their seat and would not secure their seat belt", the airline said.The delay meant the flight could not depart before the runway closed after midnight so passengers had to be rebooked on a flight the following day.The incident has split opinion about how children should be treated in such situations and how airlines should respond. Regarding the child's behaviour, Porter Airlines said "attempts by the accompanying parent and crew to address this were unsuccessful"."The aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark," it added.Child aviation safety expert Lia Tuso told the BBC the Porter crew were protecting the safety of the passengers on the flight with their decision to stop the flight, as well as the child."Unrestrained children can become projectiles," Tuso said, similar to unrestrained items of luggage, which can fly into passengers in the event of turbulence, especially during takeoff and landing. The incident has led to a debate online over how tolerant airlines should be to travelling families, and how strictly parents should enforce airline rules. Some have said it was an example of what happens when parents are too "gentle" on their children. The Fox News morning programme debated it, with co-host Charles Hurt saying he supported physical discipline. "We've all been those parents," he said.

articles.title: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
articles.excerpt: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved inFigure caption, Scammers busted in Southeast Asia's biggest ghost townByGavin ButlerReporting fromForest City, MalaysiaFrom a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that.Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust."In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties."If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better."As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract.In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people ‌and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems.From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police.Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals.

articles.title: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
articles.excerpt: On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey.But when the mighty Boeing aircraft left Ankara, the president had reportedly already been secretly spirited away via a catering truck to a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, which flew the president to RAF Mildenhall in the UK.Those left on board were unwitting decoys and had no indication that Trump was no longer travelling with them. But deception of this kind is not unusual."That's very common," said Ronald Kessler, an author who has written extensively on the agency. "There's a long history of strategies to mislead anybody who might be trying to harm the president."Robert McDonald, a former high-ranking Secret Service agent with experience working on presidential security details, told the BBC that smaller-scale deceptions are used frequently during motorcade operations.These motorcades - which often include dozens of security and support vehicles, as well as ambulances and vans carrying White House reporters - typically include two "Beasts", as the enhanced limousine carrying the president is known.While one vehicle carries the president, the other travels nearby as a decoy, switching locations while en route to the destination."It's what we call a shell game," said McDonald, who drove one of the vehicles during President George W Bush's administration. "Even in DC if we headed to Andrews [Joint Base Andrews - where Air Force One flies from], those two limousines would change position, like under a highway overpass." "But that would happen out of sight of anybody other than those in the motorcade or in that tunnel," he added. "Different things are used to mix up the bad guy."The exact nature of the perceived threat to the aircraft in this latest case remains unclear.

articles.title: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
articles.excerpt: Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure."You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally.His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali.This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake.The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city.Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead.Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete.On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise."The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor.These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below.Velasco offers hope. "In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped.""Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds."I wanted to help from the very beginning."Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens."We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says.Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock."I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know.

articles.title: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft
articles.excerpt: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar ByIndia correspondentWell past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother.Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety."Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says.An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts.The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves.By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it.Image caption, Baruah quit journalism to concentrate on animal husbandryThe scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam.The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps.The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated.For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound."This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says.Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her.

articles.title: Watch: Was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?
articles.excerpt: Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported.The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US.Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane. The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams explains.More on this story: Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say

articles.title: Watch: Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river
articles.excerpt: Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated by tropical storms, was equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas. It resulted in school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the capital. Floods, landslides and accidents driven by the rains killed at least 16 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said on Monday

articles.title: Drone captures devastating aftermath of Spokane wildfires
articles.excerpt: Severe wildfires in Spokane, Washington and surrounding areas burned 10,000 acres and destroyed more than 900 homes. Over 64,000 residents were evacuated as strong winds rapidly spread the flames.The fires became the highest firefighting priority in the US amid widespread drought and ongoing wildfires across the Pacific Northwest in early August. No serious injuries or deaths were reported in Spokane.

articles.title: Young girl finds whale stranded on Australian beach
articles.excerpt: A young girl and her mother found a humpback whale stranded at Wathumba Creek in K'gari, Queensland, Australia. The whale later self-released on the afternoon of Sunday 9 August, according to the Queensland Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation. It advises not to touch, interfere with or get close to stranded marine animals and to report them immediately.

articles.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
articles.excerpt: Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures

articles.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
articles.excerpt: Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same!

articles.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
articles.excerpt: The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding.

articles.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
articles.excerpt: The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added.

articles.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
articles.excerpt: The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star.

articles.title: Canadian airline cancels flight after child refuses to wear seatbelt
articles.excerpt: A Canadian airline cancelled a flight from Victoria to Toronto after a child refused to wear a seatbelt.The child was standing in their chair as the 6 August Porter Airlines flight taxied towards the runway, the airline said. Repeated attempts by an accompanying parent and crew to secure the child in their seat failed, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark as “the aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition”, it added.Brad Cicero, a spokesperson for the airline, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) that all passengers had to disembark, as the time needed to remove only the child and their parent and refile paperwork meant the plane could not take off before the airport closed at 12:30am.“We apologise for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day,” he told the broadcaster.Passenger Aryeh Kozuch told the Canadian Press that the child was not being unruly, and that online comments admonishing the parents did not “empathetically capture the situation”.“They just kept hiding under their seat,” he said. “If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath.”“This was a child that was in a tube with 150 people … They’re obviously terrified, and their response was to try and hide under the seat in front of them,” he said. “That’s so different than a kid running around and screaming.”Hillary Hertzberg, another passenger, said the airline could have acted faster. “It took for ever,” Hertzberg told CBC. “The kid eventually got off the plane at 11.30 so we had been on the flight for almost an hour at that point.”Porter Airlines said passengers were rebooked on a different flight the following day.

articles.title: Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country
articles.excerpt: More than 100 people died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June.The quake killed at least 132 people and more than 570 were injured as of Monday afternoon, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a group coordinating cities across the country.Rescue workers raise their fists to call for silence as they attempt to find people under the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali. Photograph: Sergio Acero/Reuters“The ⁠national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is ​needed,” Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in a national address at about 1pm local time upon declaring ‌a national state of emergency. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”Western Colombia appeared to have suffered the most serious damage. Authorities reported 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas.The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed.Map locating the epicentre of the earthquakeIn a video post, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet.

It’s now a little after midnight local time. Search and rescue efforts were under way early on Tuesday in dozens of cities and towns in western Colombia after a powerful earthquake struck the region. At least 110 people were killed after the 7.4-magnitude quake struck on Monday morning local time, toppling buildings, damaging hospitals and infrastructure and trapping people beneath the rubble in Colombia’s strongest earthquake this century. More than 2,700 people had been reported missing by Monday night. New president Abelardo de la Espriella – sworn in just days earlier – declared a state of emergency and said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”.

articles.title: ‘Shoved the tube so hard it tore my nose’: Kurdish film-maker recounts ‘inhumane’ ICE force-feeding
articles.excerpt: In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken temples and bones visible under his skin, braced himself for the immigration detention center guards to charge into his cell once again.Choli was in a solitary confinement medical cell inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in south Texas where immigrants arrested in Donald Trump’s anti-immigration crackdown are detained.Choli, a 40-year-old Kurdish asylum seeker with a thick beard and long dark hair, had been on hunger strike for over two months, demanding improved conditions for detained immigrants and to be released or deported. That day in June 2025, Choli’s nose was swollen, his throat hurt and he could still taste blood from previous days of treatment for which he never gave his consent, he said.The film-maker and activist for an independent Kurdistan has spoken out for the first time, talking exclusively to the Guardian last week from Canada about the ordeal in the United States that he said “broke him”.He recounted the vile routine as the detention center guards would rush towards him and wrestle him to the concrete cell floor, shackle his wrists and ankles, and drag him to the detention center infirmary. There, the guards pinned Choli on a bed while medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach. Choli was being force-fed by ICE.“Two guards would hold my feet; two hold my hands; one hold my head – and they would shove tubes in my nose,” Choli said. “It’s not easy to be wrestled to the ground twice a day by men that are stronger than you. And you just take it.

articles.title: Kurdish hunger striker says ICE force-feeding ‘mentally broke me’
articles.excerpt: A Kurdish man who was force-fed over the course of eight months while on hunger strike in US immigration detention has spoken out about it for the first time, describing how much the process harmed him physically and psychologically.Gabar Choli, a film-maker and activist now living in Canada after being deported, described how he endured the coercive treatment – a practice widely considered torture by international human rights groups – often twice a day after being detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when his asylum application was denied.“It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said in an exclusive interview with the Guardian. “It came to a point that I decided to write my body an apology letter.”ICE officials force-fed Choli at the Port Isabel federal detention center in Los Fresnos, south Texas, from late May 2025 until he was deported in January of this year, a Guardian investigation found. Choli had resorted to a hunger strike to protest against conditions at the facility and to push for a resolution to his immigration case.He described how a team of detention center guards would physically restrain him while ICE medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his esophagus and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach.“I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else,” Choli said. “But they were determined to break me.”Much of what happens in ICE detention has been hidden from public view over successive administrations.An investigation by the Guardian last week found that the second Trump administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures.However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. DHS sources told the Guardian over the weekend that between January 2025 and 4 August 2026 ICE obtained court orders for involuntary medical treatment for 18 hunger strikers.

articles.title: Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China
articles.excerpt: Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and central China.Forecasters warned on Tuesday that the Chinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rain over the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm.Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning.Authorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated.A person rides an electric scooter on a flooded street while avoiding fallen bicycles in Xiangyang, Hubei province. Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersThe rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines.Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country.The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media.Cars drive on a flooded street following heavy rain brought by Typhoon Dolphin in Taizhou, Zhejiang province.

articles.title: Passenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flight
articles.excerpt: China hopes to break into the world of commercial aviation with the first international flight of a Chinese-made passenger jet scheduled for Wednesday.The Comac C919 will take off from Beijing capital international airport at 3pm, landing in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, just over two hours later.It has been billed as China’s alternative to the Boeing-Airbus duopoly that dominates global aviation, particularly in Asia, but analysts say it could take generations before a Chinese aircraft could meaningfully challenge their global dominance.The C919 is made by the Chinese state-owned aircraft manufacturer Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) and is similar in size to the Boeing 737.The C919 has been flying on domestic routes operated by Chinese airlines since 2023. But Wednesday’s Air China flight to Ulaanbaatar will be the first time that the narrow-body jet is used on a commercial international route.“This is essentially a public relations move,” said Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “Ulaanbaatar was likely chosen because of how close it is to Beijing. It doesn’t change the fact that the plane was years overdue, is composed of western components, and is less efficient than its Boeing and Airbus cousins.”China has long dreamed of building its own jet. When the C919 was unveiled in 2015, Li Jiaxiang, the head of China’s civil aviation authority, said: “A great nation must have its own large commercial aircraft.”But progress has been slow, even while China has whizzed ahead in other hi-tech fields, such as robotics and electric vehicles (EVs).That is because aviation requires the integration of many different types of advanced science and engineering, as well as parts sourced from overseas.

articles.title: Thailand suspends gun licences as teen shooter and grandparents he killed are cremated
articles.excerpt: Thailand has suspended firearms licences after the deadly Nonthaburi school shooting, as the bodies of the teenage attacker and the grandparents he killed were cremated.The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, said he had ordered the interior ministry and police to stop issuing licences to possess, purchase and carry firearms, and called for “tighter controls and decisive penalties”.Anutin had vowed to implement changes on Friday when earlier that morning a 14-year-old boy shot dead the grandparents who raised him at their home in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, before killing six others at his school and then turning the gun on himself.Anutin had aimed for the reforms in previous roles as minister for the interior and health after gun violence in 2022 and 2023. He ordered a raft of gun control measures, including a short-term ban on new licences, import restrictions and the banning of people under 20 years old from shooting ranges.However, while Thailand’s licensing laws appear tough on paper, the reality is that many guns are unregistered, contributing to the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia, according to local media.

articles.title: Cook Islands election: PM Mark Brown speaks on the diplomatic crises that defined his year
articles.excerpt: As voters in the Cook Islands prepare to head to the polls in a high-stakes general election, they will have much to reflect on. Over recent years, politics in this small island nation has been defined by fierce debates about deep-sea mining, diplomatic rifts with ally New Zealand and a major reshaping of the country’s foreign partnerships.In an exclusive interview with the Guardian, days before Wednesday’s poll, Cook Islands prime minister Mark Brown defended his four-year term and the decisions he made that have seen this South Pacific nation of 17,000 people pushed into the international limelight, turning it into a battleground for influence between Beijing and western powers.In 2025, Cook Islands struck strategic partnership deals with Beijing, sparking severe alarm in Wellington. The rift was formally patched after the signing of a new bilateral agreement with New Zealand in April.Brown acknowledged the diplomatic fallout “does have bearings” on voters, saying “our people are quite mindful and aware of what happens in the geopolitical space”.Cook Islands prime minister Mark Brown on the sidelines of the G7 Summit leaders’ meeting in 2023. Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images“For us in the Cook Islands, it’s important that these engagements are on our terms … and that their collaboration with us is on areas that we’ve identified as priorities for the Cook Islands.”According to a poll conducted by Cook Islands News, Wednesday’s election will be a close race between Brown’s Cook Islands party and challenger the Cook Islands United party, led by Teariki Heather, who organised a public protest against the partnership agreement with China last year.That partnerships agreement significantly affected Cook Islanders at home and in New Zealand, Heather said, adding that Brown should have been transparent from the start about the documents signed on behalf of the country.“What prime minister Mark Brown did has upset the people.

articles.title: Weather tracker: Europe breaks more heat records as temperatures soar
articles.excerpt: High pressure has dominated central and eastern Europe in early August, breaking temperature records across the region. Austria recorded a high of 41.2C (106.2F), while Slovakia reached 42.2C. Hungary hit a peak of 41.8C, surpassing a record set in 1905, while overnight temperatures remained above 28C in some areas, marking it as a tropical night.The extreme temperatures have been driven by a heat dome beneath the high-pressure system, which traps warm air close to the surface.The prolonged heat has dried out soil and vegetation, creating conditions conducive to the spread of wildfires. Fires have burned across Italy, France, Serbia and Bulgaria, damaging forests and forcing residents to evacuate.Water levels in the Danube, which flows through much of the affected region, have fallen to an all-time low. The receding river has exposed archaeological remains and wartime wreckage, including woolly mammoth bones, second world war ships and remains associated with the Roman-era Constantine’s Bridge.Low water levels have also affected energy production, reducing the efficiency of nuclear power plants in Slovakia and Serbia and forcing Hungary to shut down a plant because there was insufficient water for cooling.Meanwhile, a buoy in the Mediterranean recorded a sea-surface temperature of 33C. If verified, it would be the highest recorded in the region.In eastern Asia, Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in China on Sunday. The national observatory had issued a red alert for the storm – the highest level – for prolonged heavy rainfall, high wind speeds and extensive damage. Dolphin has since weakened to a tropical storm.Japan is braced for Typhoon Chan-hom, just days after Dolphin swept through northern Okinawa and the Amami islands. Chan-hom is expected to make landfall near the coast of Tohoku between Tuesday and Wednesday, with up to 80mph (129km/h) gusts and an atmospheric pressure of 985 hPa.A third system, Peilou, formed on Sunday in the western Pacific.

articles.summary: 澳大利亚议会质询时间开始，反对党领袖安格斯·泰勒要求总理安东尼·阿尔巴尼斯就日本甜瓜礼盒事件泄露备忘录的争议「像个男人一样」道歉，阿尔巴尼斯则称反对党要求警方调查此事是「噱头」。众议院议长米尔顿·迪克在提前让独立议员索菲·斯卡普斯发言后承认错误，表示「我犯错误时会承认」，引发联盟党议员席的笑声。斯卡普斯此前询问政府是否会实施糖税，部长马克·巴特勒回答称目前「没有计划」像英国那样对含糖产品征税，但社区对此有不同看法，对改善包装正面标签有压倒性支持。其他关键事件包括：布拉格呼吁大幅降低最高税率档次；悉尼邦迪恐怖袭击案起诉范围扩大；澳大利亚社会服务委员会警告取消能源效率标准将「加深不平等」；独立议员提出「体育债务」方案以打击博彩广告；威尔基就博彩法案联系国家反腐败委员会，声称政府受到博彩游说团体「不当影响」；维多利亚州将为数千只小企鹅接种H5禽流感疫苗；特德·奥布莱恩就甜瓜事件向日本道歉；澳大利亚与美国、英国等签署弹道导弹试验声明；维多利亚州废除集体投票制；联邦银行录得110亿澳元创纪录利润；联盟党承诺大幅削减净海外移民和住房建设规范。

articles.title: Massive bailout for Australia’s largest aluminium smelter expected to be announced by PM and NSW premier
articles.excerpt: Anthony Albanese and the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, are preparing to mount a major bailout of Australia’s largest aluminium smelter, in a deal worth as much as $2.5bn.Resources giant Rio Tinto said in December it was contemplating ceasing operations at the Tomago aluminium smelter in NSW at the end of its current electricity supply contract.The site accounts for more than 10% of energy use in the state and employs about 1,000 workers.Albanese and Minns were expected to visit Tomago, located north-west of Newcastle, on Thursday morning to announce a joint federal-NSW funding injection, which would come as rising energy costs put the site’s immediate viability in doubt.Guardian Australia has been told the looming deal is worth $2.5bn over 10 years, with as much as $1bn in capital improvements expected from the site’s owners.Multiple sources confirmed the announcement was due to take place on Thursday morning, with the costs split 50-50 between the federal government and NSW.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Australian Financial Review first reported the looming announcement on Wednesday, linking the deal to power purchase agreements with the government-owned utility Snowy Hydro.Guardian has been told the deal will create about 2.5GW of new energy supply.The government also offered $600m to keep Glencore’s copper smelter and refinery in Mt Isa operating, as well as $240m for smelters in Hobart and Port Pirie.The bailout comes as a number of smelters prepare to switch to 100% renewable energy in the coming decade. Tomago had announced in 2021 it would “for all intents and purposes” be 100% renewable by the end of the decade.Federal Labor has offered a growing list of taxpayer-funded bailout packages to help metal processors around the country.

articles.title: Bondi shooting hero Ahmed al-Ahmed cleared of assault charges
articles.excerpt: The man who disarmed one of the gunmen allegedly responsible for the Bondi beach terror attack has had an assault case against him tossed out.Ahmed al-Ahmed, 44, had been accused of putting his father in a headlock on 9 March and intimidation over an alleged incident in June.He pleaded not guilty to both charges in an appearance at Bankstown local court on 24 June, before prosecutors confirmed on Wednesday they had withdrawn both counts.An apprehended domestic violence order protecting his father will remain in place for 12 months, court documents show.In June, his lawyer, Mohamad Sakr, emphasised al-Ahmed would maintain his innocence.“It is a family situation he never expected, one would never want to expect, and it must be really difficult for him,” he said.“He is a heroic man and his honesty and dignity should be maintained until these matters are ultimately determined.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email When the charges were initially laid, al-Ahmed alleged members of his family were seeking a cut of the $2.5m raised on his behalf after he garnered international attention for his actions during the massacre.“This situation is untrue, it’s extortion ...

articles.title: A ‘body’ found in a suitcase was actually a sex doll. How did NSW police get it so wrong?
articles.excerpt: Revelations that a “body” found inside a suitcase was actually a sex doll may have been embarrassing for police, but experts say officers followed the correct procedure.New South Wales police on Sunday were called to Oallen, a rural locality near Goulburn, after two members of the public found a suitcase containing what they believed to be human remains dumped on the side of the road.A police statement released on Sunday said the body was believed to be female, and the bag was sent to the forensic medicine laboratory.But after forensic examinations on Monday morning, it was confirmed the “body” was actually a life-like doll, understood to be a sex doll, dressed in clothes that had hair, a nose piercing and markings that resembled bruises and grazes.While former NSW police officer Vincent Hurley said the discovery was “amusing in hindsight”, investigators had done the right thing.“Police have been blamed over the years, and rightly so, for tunnel vision,” Hurley, a criminologist, told Guardian Australia.“Can you imagine if it was a real body and they just go unzip the bag and say, ‘we’ll have a poke’?“They did the right thing – it’s embarrassing, yes, but they followed procedure.”When police arrive at a reported crime scene, they generally try not to contaminate it, Hurley said.This means they may not have unzipped the bag the entire way to confirm a potential body, because doing so could destroy any fibres or blood that may have been on the zipper.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe best practice for investigating potential bodies inside things like wheelie bins and suitcases is not to open it, but to X-ray it, Paola Magni, a Murdoch University forensic science associate professor, said.Even after realising they had a doll, forensic examiners likely would have had to fully continue inspecting it for traces of evidence like semen or other DNA in case it was associated with another suspicious case.“It’s a doll, but if it’s articles.title: Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?
articles.excerpt: If you think you’ve had a bad one-night stand, spare a thought for the male redback spider, whose sole reproductive partner eats him after sex.Male redbacks appear to invite this cannibalism through a “self-sacrificial somersault”, with new research shedding light on the genetic basis of the behaviour.The redback, also known as the Australian black widow, is one of two monogynous widow spider species – meaning that males typically only mate with a single female.During copulation, a male redback uses his pedipalps – two arm-like appendages – to transfer sperm to the larger female’s two sperm storage organs. He also somersaults into the jaws of the female.“He’s pumping sperm, he flips his abdomen right over into her mouthparts and then he constricts his abdomen … to make it hard for the female to get a purchase on his abdomen. That lets him survive the first mating,” said Cor Vink, an associate professor and spider expert at Lincoln University in New Zealand.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe self-sacrificial flip is thought to help maximise reproductive success, but the males risk being eaten before they are able to transfer sperm to the female’s second storage organ.“Ideally, males should mate with the same female two times because females have two separate sperm storage organs,” said Kardelen Özgün Uludag of the University of Hamburg, the study’s first author.“A male needs to inseminate and plug both of them, so that he can sire all of the offspring she produces.“If a male dies after the first mating, another male can mate with the same female and then half of the female’s offspring would be from the second male.”To avoid becoming a post-coital meal, previous research has found that some males have developed the survival tactic of mating with immature females not yet experienced in eating their partners.A female redback. Of the 31 species of widow spider, male sacrificial behaviour is only usually observed in redbacks and brown widows.

articles.title: UK heatwaves may have cost economy £4.4bn in lost output so far this year, analysis finds
articles.excerpt: Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, new analysis shows.Green thinktank Verdant had suggested June’s unseasonally hot weather had an economic cost of £2.36bn. Updating its assessment to include last month’s high temperatures, it finds a £4.4bn hit to output.As temperatures soar once again this week, Verdant’s director, James Meadway, said: “The economic costs of climate change are already with us, and set to worsen in future years. Action by the government to protect workers and businesses from the severe effects of extreme heat is well overdue.”Direct economic costs arise because workers across many industries become less productive in heatwaves, while infrastructure and equipment overheats and has to be shut down.This week’s amber weather warning for extreme heat in England from the Met Office, comes after three previous heatwaves in the UK in May, June and July. The forecaster has said the UK is on course to record its hottest summer ever.Verdant is calling for the government to implement a maximum working temperature; and be ready to step in to compensate workers when they are forced to cut their hours because of extreme heat.The report also points to the need for investment in urban redesign, to create more cooler green spaces in the UK’s towns and cities.Verdant’s estimates exclude indirect losses such as the cost of fighting wildfires, and additional electricity consumption from running fans and air conditioning.

articles.title: British man with dementia told to leave Sweden after losing migration case
articles.excerpt: A 74-year-old British man who has been living in Sweden for 25 years who needs round-the-clock care for dementia has been given 10 days to leave the country after he lost a post-Brexit migration court case.The deportation order comes after a Swedish court ruling in July that the government’s drive to reduce immigration trumped the needs of a man in full-time care.“The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace Mason’s interest in continuing to reside” in Sweden, the migrations court of appeals ruled in July.The Masons’ family trauma echoes that of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who the Guardian revealed on Monday was also facing deportation because of late Brexit paperwork despite living in Sweden for 21 years.The son of Horace Mason (known as George) was told by the British embassy on Friday the authorities had given him until 20 August.“It made me feel sick. We’ve been trying to keep as much information from him as possibly because with the illness he is confused and worried.“But I had to tell him on Friday what had happened and there was just a thousand questions: ‘What is going to happen? Are the police going to come and take me away. Are they going to kick the door down?’George Mason with his son Carl. Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family“I had dinner with him again today [Monday] and it was the same: ‘What is going to happen now? Where am I going to go in England? Are they going to arrest me and put me in prison.“It’s inhumane,” his son Carl said.The UK government said it was aware of the case.“We are supporting Mr Mason and his family and are in contact with the Swedish authorities about his case.”Mason’s case comes two years after another Briton, Kathleen Poole, also suffering dementia was threatened with deportation before she died in a care home.Mason moved to Sweden from Hinckley in Leicestershire to be close to his son and grandchildren around the year 2000.“He is elderly and extremely vulnerable.
