articles.title: US military fires on cargo vessel it said sought to break Iran blockade
articles.excerpt: CENTCOM says helicopter fired at engine room of Panama-flagged Vela Nova as US-Iran diplomacy remains stalled.The United States military has said it fired on a ship attempting to break its blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman.The attack on Tuesday comes amid a period of relative calm in the US-Israeli war with Iran, with attacks mostly paused since a 13-day escalation in July. That came after a ceasefire as part of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran in June appeared to collapse.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump took ‘secret flight’ from Turkiye to avoid Iran ‘threat’list 2 of 3Trump sends conflicting signals on Iran strategylist 3 of 3Iran, US set new conditions during Hormuz talks: What does this mean?end of listIn a statement, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees the Middle East, said a Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged Vela Nova cargo vessel.It said the vessel “attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman and violate the U.S. blockade against Iran by sailing toward an Iranian port”.The attack targeted the ship’s engine room and disabled its steering gear, CENTCOM said, alleging the crew “ignored repeated warnings from American forces”.It did not say if any crew members were wounded in the attack. In its statement on Tuesday, CENTCOM said US forces had disabled 55 commercial vessels throughout its blockade on Iranian ports, disabled three “non-compliant vessels”, and boarded two.The US reimposed its naval blockade of Iranian ports amid the recent return to fighting, with Iran again reasserting its control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Victims were rushed to hospital in the nearby town of El-Kassasin.“Most of the dead are children 13 and 14 years old,” a medical source at the hospital told AFP. The youngest victim was 10 years oldThe workers were mostly from two villages in Sharqiya governorate and were employed on a farm in Ismailia, a local security source said.President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi had ordered an investigation into the accident and the Ministry of Social Solidarity and Ministry of Labour said it would provide financial assistance to the families of those killed and to injured workers.Pick-up trucks are a common way for Egypt’s informal workers to reach their jobs. articles.title: Armistice Regime, Peace Regime, or Time for a Different Mindset on the Korean Peninsula?
articles.excerpt: On the 73rd anniversary of the Korean Armistice Agreement late last month, South Korea’s Minister of Unification Chung Dong-young declared, “We must end the Armistice regime and move to a peace regime.” His statement echoed a promise from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, who earlier in July promised South Korea’s Peace Unification Advisory Council that his administration would work to transition the Korean Peninsula away from the Armistice Agreement toward a “peace regime” paradigm. But what does this actually mean? What is a “peace regime” and is it attainable with North Korea? These questions matter because they inform the trajectory of South Korea’s policy toward the North and, more fundamentally, how policymakers in Seoul approach peacebuilding on the peninsula. In short, the “peace regime” is a long-standing South Korean policy design aimed at establishing a new framework for inter-Korean relations. The operative notion is to transition from the Armistice Agreement to an inter-Korean peace arrangement, to reduce foreign interference in the Korean peace process, and to establish interdependencies that would advance the two countries toward eventual reunification. While at times showing early promise during brief periods of rapprochement, this approach has ultimately been unable to achieve these objectives. This is principally owing to the fundamental mismatch with North Korea’s policy preferences and domestic politics in South Korea. But the treatment of the peace process as discrete phases also runs contrary to the basic principles of peacebuilding, installing arbitrary friction points and creating missed opportunities for shared cooperation. Effective inter-Korean policy will eventually require a reframing of the peacebuilding efforts on the Korean Peninsula.

articles.title: When Is a Central Asian Leaders Summit Not a Summit?
articles.excerpt: Kyrgyzstan has been earning its long-time moniker as the “Switzerland” of Central Asia of late, having already hosted a flurry of senior diplomatic visits this summer, ahead of a busy few weeks that will see the Shanghai Cooperation Organization celebrate its 25th anniversary with a summit in Bishkek, and the biannual World Nomad Games again setting up camp on the banks of Issyk-Kul. In regional terms, the most significant of these visits to Kyrgyzstan arguably came at the end of July, when the five leaders of the Central Asian republics were joined by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev at the resort town of Cholpon-Ata for a high-level get-together. This was the group’s first gathering since November 2025, when Baku was formally welcomed as a participant at the seventh official Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia, the region’s annual leaders summit.. At first glance, the one-day summit had all of the hallmarks of a typical Consultative Meeting. It was used as an opportunity to announce trade deals — such as the expansion of the Kyrgyz-Azerbaijani Development Fund from $100 million to $200 million — and featured the platitudes regularly offered and proposals regularly made by Central Asia’s presidents. Uzbekistan’s leader, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, for example, commended Kyrgyzstan on its recent election as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, paid tribute to the “common regional identity” taking shape, and stressed the importance of strengthening interstate coordination via the “Central Asia Plus” negotiating format. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, meanwhile, suggested the building of a large regional oil refinery — likely on the back of Central Asia’s recent fuel crisis, which has been especially acute in Tajikistan. The only problem is that what happened at Cholpon-Ata wasn’t a Consultative Meeting at all.

articles.title: ‘Golden Kamuy’ and Modern Russo-Japanese Relations
articles.excerpt: Spoiler Alert: Key plot points in “Golden Kamuy” discussed in detail below. Modern-day relations between Japan and Russia are complex, with one of the most pivotal turning points in the relationship being the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War. While the conflict has been extensively studied in academic literature, a popular manga and anime known as “Golden Kamuy” uses the backdrop of the Russo-Japanese War to reevaluate Russo-Japanese relations more broadly, as well as the status of the Ainu and other indigenous Far Eastern people. “Golden Kamuy,” created by Noda Satoru, ran as a serialized manga from 2014 to 2022. It then spawned a five-season anime series, with its final segment expected to wrap up in late 2026, and several live-action movies. “Golden Kamuy” focuses on Sugimoto Saichi, a veteran of the Russo-Japanese War, and an Ainu girl named Asirpa. The two team up in search of a hidden treasure trove of gold, but they have to piece together a map tattooed across the backs of 24 prisoners who escaped from Abashiri prison. The duo encounters both allies and enemies in their quest. Location plays a leading role in “Golden Kamuy”: most of the action takes place in Hokkaido, today the northernmost island of Japan and historically the homeland of the Ainu people. A prominent subplot also brings the main characters to Sakhalin, a Russo-Japanese borderland that is today Russian territory; the area has also long been settled by indigenous Ainu, Nivkh, and Uilta/Orok peoples. The interplay of Japanese, Russian, and Ainu cultures in the show, especially as territorial claims changed hands (most notably in the case of Sakhalin), drives the plot forward and showcases how those interactions continue to shape relations in this part of the world today. In addition, “Golden Kamuy” inserts itself into pivotal moments of Russian and Japanese history by weaving its narrative into real-life historical events.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact and America’s Reduced Leverage in West Asia
articles.excerpt: The signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye on August 7 is a significant development. The pact is the first formal regional security agreement to be formed as a direct result of the conflict between the U.S. and Iran. The agreement reflects the lessons that key regional actors have drawn from the crisis as they seek to redefine their place within a security order long dominated by the U.S. The West Asia war has revealed that the American defense umbrella in the form of forward bases in the region is not adequate in protecting Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf Arab states from Iranian attacks. Rather, the U.S. military presence in these states pulled them directly into the conflict, making them targets of Iran and its regional allies. Additionally, the Israeli military’s approach to the Palestinian question and its bombing of the people of Gaza have drawn widespread ire in the Muslim world. For decades, Washington served as the sole security guarantor in the Gulf. The emergence of a formal defense pact among key regional players that excludes the U.S. is may chip away at Washington’s leverage in the region. While this erosion of influence may not become fully apparent in the short term, it is likely to assume greater significance in the coming years, particularly with respect to arms sales, the negotiation of military basing rights, and the management of regional crises. One may argue that as a result of the pact the U.S. will now be indirectly constrained by decisions taken jointly by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. For instance, the Mecca Pact stipulates that an attack on one country will be regarded as an attack upon all. While the signatories have not publicly elaborated the precise circumstances under which the idea of collective commitment would be activated, it is reasonable to conclude that they have reached internal understandings regarding the scenarios that would trigger such a response.

articles.title: Why the Pacific Islands Forum Should Watch Taiwan’s East Coast
articles.excerpt: Ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), scheduled to take place August 30 to September 4 in Palau, Pacific Island leaders failed to reach consensus on a joint statement criticizing China’s submarine-based ballistic missile testing in the Pacific. The split reflects intensifying great-power competition and divergent threat perceptions between external powers and Pacific governments. Yet China’s growing military activities have clearly heightened concerns among forum members. Besides missile testing, another less visible source of pressure lies in the growing normalization of Chinese naval and coast guard activity in the waters east of Taiwan, a development the PIF has yet to fully connect to its own maritime interests. This maritime gateway east of Taiwan leads directly into the exclusive economic zones that the forum seeks to protect and deserves greater attention from Pacific Island states. Rather than a distant flashpoint, the waters east of Taiwan form the northern hinge of the same maritime arc that runs through Micronesia and Melanesia, linked by overlapping sea lines of communication and interconnected ocean current systems. This deep-water gateway to the Blue Pacific is increasingly being trespassed and pressured by Chinese government vessels. Beijing appears to be using unresolved maritime boundary negotiations involving Japan and the Philippines as justification for expanding coast guard patrols and deploying more research and survey vessels east of Taiwan. Many of these platforms are converted former naval vessels, underscoring the increasingly blurred line between maritime law enforcement and strategic power projection. By increasing the frequency and persistence of deployments along Taiwan’s Pacific coast, Beijing appears to be seeking to normalize a sustained Chinese maritime security presence in the Blue Pacific waters. This expansion is unfolding alongside a broader rise in Chinese naval activity in the Western Pacific.

articles.title: Symbolic Concessions, No Implementation: Myanmar’s Promises of Rohingya Repatriation
articles.excerpt: ASEAN Beat | Diplomacy | Southeast Asia Myanmar’s latest pledge to repatriate 300,000 Rohingya refugees cannot be viewed as a credible commitment. It’s yet another iteration of a well-established diplomatic pattern. Rohingya children gather sticks at a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, March 2018. Credit: UN Women/Alison Joyce On July 29, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim remarked that Myanmar had agreed to repatriate 300,000 Rohingya refugees from Bangladesh and 5,000 from Malaysia. Subsequently, Malaysian and Bangladeshi media outlets enthusiastically disseminated the news. However, the very next day, Bangladeshi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed stated that Myanmar had forwarded no such proposal to Bangladesh, and while the two sides maintain contact, the topic of the repatriation of 300,000 refugees has not been discussed. While people may be tempted to view this event in the context of the domestic politics of Malaysia, it, in fact, confirms a long-standing pattern of behavior on the part of the Myanmar government toward the protracted Rohingya crisis. In 2017-2018, the Myanmar government orchestrated “cleansing operations” in northern Rakhine State, leading to the exodus of more than 750,000 Rohingyas to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined some 300,000 Rohingya refugees, who had been residing in Bangladesh since the late 1970s or the 1990s. The exodus of the Rohingyas was accompanied by disturbing reports of war crimes — massacres, sexual assaults, arson, plunder, and others — committed by the Myanmar military, the Tatmadaw, against the Rohingya. The United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) deemed Myanmar’s actions to be “ethnic cleansing,” while the United States recognized it as a “genocide.” Currently, Bangladesh hosts some 1.5 million Rohingya refugees, making it one of the largest hosts of refugees anywhere in the world.

articles.title: Reclaiming the Backyard: ASEAN’s Realpolitik Push on Myanmar
articles.excerpt: In late 2025, nearly five years after the February 2021 coup, the military junta held a multi-phase election. The polls, which were heavily skewed in favor of the military, produced the expected outcome: the military proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party won 232 of 263 seats in the lower house of the Union Parliament and 109 of 157 seats in the upper house. The election was intended to put a thin veneer of legitimacy on the military dictatorship in order to gain partial re-entry into the international community while continuing its war against the country’s resistance elements. Following the military-administered election, Min Aung Hlaing officially assumed the presidency in April 2026, framing the transition as the constitutional fulfillment of a return to civilian governance. This domestic political shift inaugurated a carefully orchestrated diplomatic campaign across key neighboring states, which took Min Aung Hlaing to India, Laos, China, and Thailand, designed to launder regime legitimacy, secure critical border trade, and hedge against Western sanctions. Rather than signaling a complete resolution of domestic conflicts, this regional pivot reflects a strategic calibration by neighboring Asian powers that prioritize border stability, maritime security, and economic corridors over concerns about Myanmar’s internal affairs. From the perspective of the administration in Naypyidaw, the formal transition to a civilian government under the 2008 Constitution provides an exit ramp from pariah status toward institutional normalization. To facilitate this regional re-engagement, the government made a number of strategic, low-cost domestic concessions. Most notably, in late April, it moved Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi from prison to house arrest in an effort to soften regional criticism without surrendering any real executive authority.

articles.title: Indonesia’s President Nominates Central Bank Deputy as New Governor
articles.excerpt: Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto has nominated Destry Damayanti, a long-time central bank deputy, as the next governor of the institution, an official announced yesterday. State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi confirmed that the nomination was submitted to the House of Representatives through a presidential letter, along with names of nominees for Bank of Indonesia (BI)’s senior deputy role, which Destry previously filled. Destry Damayanti, a seasoned economist and former chief economist at the state lender Bank Mandiri, has served as the interim governor of BI since the unexpected resignation of Perry Warjiyo last month for “personal reasons.” Perry had served as BI’s governor of the central bank since 2018 and still had three years to run on his term. Both appointments must be approved by lawmakers, but given the size of Prabowo’s majority in the House, this is likely to be little more than a formality. If (or when) she is approved, Destry, who has also worked for Citibank and served on the board of commissioners for the Indonesia Deposit Insurance Corporation, will become the first woman to take on the role on a permanent basis. The announcement delivered a small fillip to the rupiah, which closed yesterday at 17,755 to the U.S. dollar, gaining 142 points, or 0.79 percent, from its previous close of 17,897. The markets’ response hints at the fragile state of investor confidence in Indonesia. Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has pursued high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, which have widened the fiscal deficit and pushed it toward its legally mandated ceiling of 3 percent of GDP. The former general has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s return from natural resources and international trade.

articles.title: Art, Surveillance, and the Politics of Memory in Southeast Asia
articles.excerpt: Across Southeast Asia, artists and cultural rights defenders are increasingly being cast as threats – to public morality, political order and dominant narratives about gender, sexuality, identity, and belonging. This is especially true for queer and trans artists, whose bodies, stories, and performances often challenge the boundaries that states, religious authorities, and conservative movements seek to impose. When they are surveilled or attacked, or their work is censored, the consequences touch the foundations of civic space: the right to speak, gather, remember, imagine, and contest power. ArtsEquator’s Southeast Asia Artistic Freedom RADAR Database documents this reality across Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. In its 2025 report, RADAR recorded 159 challenges to artistic freedom across the seven countries. The findings closely mirror those of the CIVICUS Monitor, which rated Myanmar and Vietnam as “Closed,” Cambodia, Thailand, and the Philippines as “Repressed,” and Malaysia and Indonesia as “Obstructed.” This matters because attacks on artistic freedom often serve as warnings about the health of civic life. Where artists are censored, surveilled, attacked, or forced into silence, broader patterns of repression are already at work. While navigating the RADAR database, I came across “moral policing” as a category of violations faced by artists and cultural rights workers. In practice, moral policing punishes artists and communities whose work challenges artificial boundaries around gender, sexuality, faith, tradition, or national identity. It does not always manifest as an outright ban or formal legal charge. More often, it takes shape through public accusations, social pressure, police scrutiny, cancelled performances, restrictions on distribution, withdrawal of support, online harassment, physical attacks, surveillance, or the destruction of artworks.

articles.title: ASEAN Fractures Widen as Thailand Hosts Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing
articles.excerpt: Beyond the Mekong | Diplomacy | Southeast Asia A conversation with Mark Cogan of Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka. As the people of Myanmar recently commemorated the 8888 uprising that demanded political freedom but was brutally put down in August 1988, Thailand was playing host to Min Aung Hlaing, the former general who seized power through a coup in early 2021. This was Min Aung Hlaing’s second official visit to an ASEAN member state since military-staged elections in December and January ensured his transition to the presidency and one that widened the schisms within ASEAN, which has barred Myanmar from official summits and events amid a bloody civil war. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul broke with that line despite ASEAN protocols and potential legal issues given the International Court of Justice will soon deliver its verdict on whether Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s senior generals committed a genocide against the Rohingya. Min Aung Hlaing’s first official visit as president was to Laos in early July and his trip to Thailand came less than a week after he allowed a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross to meet with the jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who had been unsighted for many years amid concerns for her health. Mark Cogan is an associate professor of Peace and Conflict Studies at Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka and a regular contributor to The Diplomat. He joined Luke Hunt on Beyond the Mekong to discuss the recent developments in regional politics. That includes the moral and political questions that have divided maritime and mainland Southeast Asia, including the civil war in Myanmar, which has claimed 100,000 lives, the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, and Thailand’s simmering border conflict with Cambodia.

articles.title: US Official Reassures Asia of Commitment, Calls for Greater Burden Sharing
articles.excerpt: The United States remains strongly committed to Asia but wants its partners to bear more of the burden for their own defense, a senior Pentagon official said in the Philippines yesterday. Seeking to counter concerns about Washington’s reliability, given the capricious character of U.S. foreign policy under the second Trump administration, Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby said that U.S. interests were “more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.” “America is definitely not disengaging from Asia,” Colby said in a speech in Manila. “We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most.” Colby made the remarks at a forum in the Philippines, his first stop on a Southeast Asian tour that will also take him and Assistant Secretary of War John Noh to Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia. In a statement, the Department of War said that trip, which will involve meetings with senior officials in each country, “reaffirms the Department’s commitment to build a durable peace in the region through strength.” During the trip, Colby said in his Manila speech, he intended to “deliver a clear message that is at once both realistic and perhaps bracing but also reassuring: That America’s interests are more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific, and that we at the Department of War are concentrated on ensuring those interests are stoutly defended.” Colby said maintaining a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific required a “posture of deterrence by denial along the First Island Chain,” the barrier of islands that stretches from Japan down to Taiwan, the Philippines, and the northern coast of Borneo. He pointed to what he said was a growing U.S. military commitment in the region, which has involved the deployment of additional troops, ships, aircraft, and missile systems throughout the First Island Chain.

articles.title: Painting Bullseyes: What Iran’s Attacks on US Bases Mean for the Indo-Pacific
articles.excerpt: The United States maintains the world’s largest overseas military basing presence, with as many as 750 installations in 80 countries. Most recently, U.S. bases and bases to which the U.S. military has access in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have become the targets of Iranian attacks, in retaliation for U.S. strikes on the country. These attacks have not only resulted in the deaths of several U.S. soldiers, but have impacted local residents in proximity to the bases and pushed others to question the necessity of the U.S. bases entirely. Analysts have speculated about what these attacks and the subsequent damages to the bases might mean for U.S. basing in the region, including potential base closures. But what does Iran’s targeting of U.S. bases and the resulting destruction mean for the rest of the 80 countries that host the U.S. military? This is an especially salient question for the host countries in the Indo-Pacific, where the specter of a U.S.-China confrontation looms large and U.S. security partners in the region maintain some of the largest troop deployments in the world, with Japan and South Korea hosting the largest and third largest deployments, respectively. The attacks in the Middle East have raised anxieties elsewhere, as residents of communities near U.S. bases the world over worry about becoming the target of external aggression. In the wake of Iran’s attacks, for instance, some Philippine policymakers have expressed concerns that by providing the U.S. with basing access, the Philippine government is “effectively painting bullseyes on Filipino soil” vis-à-vis China. Such concerns are not new in the Indo-Pacific, although the events in the Middle East may make the prospects of U.S. bases serving as targets more tangible to citizens in the host countries in the region. articles.title: Air Force Ascendant: Senior PLA Leadership Changes and Their Implications
articles.excerpt: Amid leadership disruption caused by the purges, the reconstruction of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) high command is underway. Recent reports by the South China Morning Post and Channel News Asia indicate that officers from the PLA Air Force (PLAAF) have recently risen to senior leadership positions, prompting renewed discussions on the significance of this development. At present, PLAAF officers are in charge of five Central Military Commission (CMC) departments, compared with seven headed by Army officers, making the PLAAF the second-best-represented service at the CMC level. Moreover, of the PLA’s five theater commands, PLAAF officers lead two: the Eastern and Central Theater Commands. Meanwhile, an Army lieutenant general heads the Northern Theater Command, while a Navy vice admiral leads the Southern Theater Command. The situation within the Western Theater Command is murkier. Its commander, an Army general, has been missing for many months and his PLAAF deputy appears to have taken up some of his responsibilities. Overall, the expanding PLAAF presence at the top of the PLA hierarchy is obvious. If current trends continue, the PLAAF is likely going to have a greater-than-usual presence on the next CMC, whose composition is expected to be confirmed at the 21st Party Congress in 2027. This development has the potential to reshape the PLA in multiple ways, rendering an analysis of the PLAAF’s rise and its wider implications worthy. The PLAAF’s representation on the CMC has historically been limited. In the Xi Jinping era, only two PLAAF officers served as CMC members: PLAAF Commander Ma Xiaotian from 2012 to 2017, and Air Force General Xu Qiliang as the CMC vice chairman from 2012 to 2022. Only one PLAAF officer served as the director of a CMC department: Air Force General Xu Xueqiang, who led the Equipment Development Department from 2022 until 2026. However, the limited representation may have been a blessing in disguise.

articles.title: Safeguarding Storage: Wildberries’ Move to Kazakhstan
articles.excerpt: On August 4, Kazakhstani Minister for Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev announced that the Russian e-commerce platform Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in the country. According to the minister, Wildberries plans to build 260,000 square meters of storage, split between Astana and Almaty, expanding its capacity more than eightfold from its current 46,000 square meters of leased warehouse space. The announcement comes following a July marked by more than 20 attacks on Wildberries’ logistical hubs across Russia, also affecting Kazakh sellers on the platform who have lost an estimated $3.2 million worth of goods. Despite media reports framing the expansion as a relocation of the e-commerce platform, the planned warehouses in Kazakhstan would not be able to cover the more than 1 million square meters lost over the last month. On top of this, Wildberries’ new warehouses planned in Kazakhstan are, at the time of writing, only set to be completed in 2027, thereby not solving the current problems facing the company. This news, however, came just days after the Russian newspaper cited multiple sources saying the company was looking for 100,000 square meters of extra storage. Wildberries’ overall aim to build more warehouses in Kazakhstan is not new. In fact, such an effort announced at the beginning of 2023, with plans to open two years later before the project was postponed. The company’s market share in Kazakhstan has grown, now making it a distant second with almost 27 percent of the e-commerce market. Locally founded Kaspi keeps almost two-thirds of the market. Wildberries is reportedly scrambling to find an additional 100,000 square meters of warehouse space as a result of the last month’s many attacks. Reports of this new search for space came as it became clear that losses at Wildberries hubs in Russia could amount to upward of $3.37 billion.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact Extends Pakistan’s Security Role Westward
articles.excerpt: At the time of their exploratory trilateral talks in February, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan had no formal defense commitment. It was unclear whether the discussions would produce much beyond political coordination. That has now changed. On August 7, the three governments signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. Its main provision stipulates that an armed attack on one party will be regarded as an attack on all three. Yet the public account of the agreement leaves the resulting military obligations undefined. There is no disclosed procedure for deciding that an attack has triggered the pact, no announced geographical limit, and no public explanation of what assistance each country must provide. The comparison with NATO’s Article 5 is useful, but only in a limited sense. Article 5 leaves each ally discretion over the action it considers necessary. NATO also has decades of military planning and cooperation behind it. Nothing comparable has yet been publicly disclosed for the Mecca pact. Saudi Arabia has made similar attempts before. The Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, announced in 2015, eventually brought together 41 states under a Saudi-led structure. A former Pakistani army chief, Raheel Sharif, became its military commander. Participation still depended on each country’s own decisions, and member sovereignty was explicitly preserved. This history makes the “Muslim NATO” label for the Mecca pact premature. Mecca has far fewer members, but its mutual-defense pledge does go much further. Pakistan has already shown what a defense commitment to Saudi Arabia can mean in practice. During the spring phase of the Iran war earlier this year, Islamabad deployed a reported 8,000 troops, JF-17 fighters, drones, and a Chinese HQ-9 air-defense system to Saudi Arabia under the bilateral 2025 Saudi-Pakistani defense agreement. Pakistani personnel operated the equipment while Saudi Arabia financed the deployment.

articles.title: Austria Says No to the Tajik Government
articles.excerpt: A criminal court in Vienna on August 5 refused Tajikistan’s request to extradite Shavkat Muhammad, a member of the banned National Alliance of Tajikistan, along with his 77-year-old mother, Sharofat Sharifova, and his brother Bilolidin Sharifov. Tajik authorities accuse the three of extremism; the family calls the prosecution political. No written ruling has been published, and the account of the hearing comes from opposition figures who were in the room. This is the fourth refusal to come out of a single Tajik submission. In April, the Interior Ministry sent Austria’s Justice Ministry files on 18 members of exiled opposition organizations, a dossier Leila Nazgul Seiitbek examined for the Diplomat in June. On June 24, a Vienna court took up the case of Islamic Renaissance Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) member Firdavs Shukurov. The conduct Dushanbe cited in its own case materials was Shukurov holding an anti-Rahmon banner at an October 2021 demonstration in Vienna, partly documented in a YouTube video. The rally had been authorized and Shukurov held refugee status. Five days later the same court blocked the return of a 49-year-old woman wanted since 2018 for public calls to change the constitutional order. Austria has not always drawn a firm line on these kinds of requests, and the difference appears to have been procedural. In March 2020 it removed Hizbullo Shovalizoda after rejecting his asylum claim, a migration decision rather than an extradition ruling. He was detained on arrival in Dushanbe and sentenced in June to 20 years for treason and participation in an extremist organization in a closed trial. An Austrian court later invalidated the removal, finding that the asylum decision had relied on outdated information about conditions in Tajikistan, and obliged Vienna to bring him back. He is still in prison.

articles.title: The China-Russia-North Korea Authoritarian Axis Looms Over Wars in Ukraine and Iran
articles.excerpt: China’s reported sale of shoulder-launched missile systems to Iran should be concerning not just to the United States but also to Australia and other major powers in the Indo-Pacific. It demonstrates a deeper strategic partnership between Beijing and Tehran – one with destabilizing consequences for the Middle East – and shows a certain recklessness in Chinese behavior. But China is not alone in this endeavor. Russia is an active party aiding Iran in a variety of ways, even though it has its hands full with its ill-advised invasion of Ukraine. Sino-Russian assistance to Iran degrades the international security situation in the Middle East and worsens the Strait of Hormuz crisis. And North Korea is involved too, completing the authoritarian axis. According to a July 29 Reuters report, the China-Iran weapons contract is for shoulder-fired missile systems – up to 400 QW-12 and FN-16 man-portable air defense systems – under a deal worth between $60 million and $70 million. The missile systems could help Iran rebuild short-range air defenses, which have been severely degraded after five months of Israeli-U.S. military strikes. To hide its role, China reportedly had a Hong Kong-based company, Zhongqing Baoshang International Investment, act as a middle agent facilitating the deal with Iran. China’s Foreign Ministry rejected the reports, saying that they had “no factual ground at all.” The Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson also added that “China always works for peace and the end of the conflict.” China’s Defense Ministry spokesperson made a similar statement saying that he was “not familiar with the relevant situation.” This isn’t the first time reports about China’s sale of missile systems have become public. In February, Reuters reported that Iran and China were closing a deal for the sale of Chinese CM-302 supersonic anti-ship missiles. With a 290 km range, these were meant to boost Iran’s strike capabilities against the U.S. navy.

articles.title: Samsung, SK Hynix Tests of Chinese Chip Tools Expose Cracks in US Export Strategy
articles.excerpt: Pacific Money | Economy | East Asia South Korean chipmakers are evaluating Chinese equipment as a hedge against shifting export rules from Washington. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two largest global memory chipmakers, have spent roughly two years testing chipmaking equipment from the Chinese firm Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. (AMEC), according to local news reports. The trials, first reported by Reuters on August 5, amount to a hedge against tightening U.S. export controls that could eventually cut Western companies off from servicing tools already installed inside the two firms’ Chinese factories. Samsung has denied testing AMEC equipment at its China site or considering such a test, and SK Hynix has not commented on the matter. Even so, engineers at both companies began qualifying AMEC’s etching tools around two years ago. At the time, it was unclear whether Washington would keep allowing imports of U.S. chipmaking equipment into China. In 2023, the U.S. Commerce Department designated Samsung and SK Hynix’s Chinese factories as validated end users. The status let the companies import certain controlled American equipment without applying for a license each time. However, Washington revoked the status in 2025, then granted both firms a narrower annual license covering equipment imports for 2026. Each policy swing left the two chipmakers less certain their existing American and Dutch tools would keep receiving spare parts, software updates, and repair support. Memory-chip production lines depend on equipment calibrated with extreme precision and supplier uncertainty is difficult for a fab to absorb. Alongside tightening U.S. export controls, China’s chipmaking industry has been making rapid strides. A state-backed manufacturer based in Shanghai began mass-producing immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines in late July, aiming to deliver roughly five units this year and about 20 in 2027 to three of the country’s leading chipmakers.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina’s Media Event in India Hits Bangladesh-India Ties
articles.excerpt: New Delhi’s decision to allow deposed Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to hold a press conference on August 5, coinciding with the second anniversary of the toppling of her government in a student uprising in 2024, has set back India’s ties with the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government in Dhaka. What is most intriguing is the timing. Ties with the Tarique Rahman-led government were on the mend as Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr. Khalilur Rahman visited New Delhi from April 7 to 9, marking the first high-level ministerial engagement. India too had sent an invitation to Prime Minister Rahman to attend the BRICS summit to be held in New Delhi in September. Bilateral trade and the issuing of visas to Bangladeshi citizens had resumed. The appointment of Dinesh Trivedi, a senior politician, as India’s new high commissioner was seen as a thawing of frozen ties. All these measures took a hit when Sheikh Hasina was allowed to hold a press conference. India’s foreign ministry distanced itself from the event, with a ministry spokesman saying the government had no role to play in what was an event by a private media entity, and that the government does not endorse anything said at the forum. Even so, especially with regard to the duly constituted government of Bangladesh, the damage was done. The press event prompted a furious reaction from Dhaka. The government expressed deep outrage and regret, describing the incident as a direct affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution. The foreign ministry press note further warned of the severe ramifications such a public platform could have on the reset and restoration of bilateral relations. Bangladesh has already sought Sheikh Hasina’s extradition under the 2013 India-Bangladesh Extradition Treaty. Hasina’s son Sajeeb Wazed Joy further aggravated the situation by calling Bangladesh a “failed state” and saying it could emerge as a hub for regional terrorism.

articles.title: Southeast Asia’s Border Disputes: Wars in Waiting?
articles.excerpt: Videos | Security | Southeast Asia The region’s maritime borders are hotly contested, but on land there’s the real risk of conflict, too. You probably have heard of the South China Sea disputes – a major flashpoint involving China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Brunei. But the South China Sea isn’t the only dispute threatening to spark a war in Southeast Asia. There are plenty more contested borders on land as well. Today, we’re going to talk about three other territorial disputes in the region – the kind of flashpoints that stay below the headlines until it’s too late. Stay tuned, because we’re ranking them in order: from the least likely to spark an actual shooting war to the highest risk of conflict. In fact, one of these disputes even flared into a full-blown shooting war in 2025 – and it could happen again at any time.

articles.title: Bangladesh Joins Saudi-led Defense Coalition as Bab el-Mandeb Risks Grow
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh has joined a Saudi-led maritime defense coalition amid rising tensions in West Asia, which are putting some of the world’s busiest shipping routes via the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden at risk. The coalition has 14 founding members: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Pakistan, Turkiye, Egypt, Jordan, Yemen, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Sudan, Djibouti, and Somalia. Saudi Arabia will lead the coalition and host its headquarters. Its planned activities include intelligence sharing, joint planning, and coordinated maritime operations. However, its charter, command system and rules of engagement have not yet been made public. The initiative followed attacks on Saudi-linked shipping and a naval blockade announced by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement on July 20. The threat became more serious after disruption in the Strait of Hormuz pushed Saudi Arabia to move more oil through Yanbu, its main port on the Red Sea. This placed greater pressure on the route through Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia now faces risks around both of the main waterways used to move energy supplies from the Arabian Peninsula. Bangladesh has backed the coalition, which aims to strengthen maritime security and protect freedom of navigation, international trade routes, and energy supply lines. Dhaka had condemned the Houthi blockade on July 22, warning that it could threaten regional peace and stability and disrupt global trade and energy supplies. Its decision to join the coalition reflects Bangladesh’s own exposure to trouble in the region. Bangladesh sends a large share of its exports to Europe. Ships carrying garments and other goods normally use the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. When shipping companies avoid this route, vessels must travel around the Cape of Good Hope. The longer journey increases fuel use, freight charges, insurance costs, and delivery times.

articles.title: Why Pakistan Is Pleased With Its Counterterrorism Dialogue With the US
articles.excerpt: Pakistan and the United States held the fourth round of their annual Counterterrorism Dialogue in Washington, D.C., on August 4. The Pakistani delegation was led by Ambassador Nabeel Munir, special secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, while Ambassador Gregory LoGerfo, the U.S. coordinator for counterterrorism, led the American side. The joint statement issued at the end of the talks underscored their shared strategic interests in the counterterrorism partnership and determination to confront regional security threats. “The United States and Pakistan affirmed their joint resolve to confront terrorist organizations that endanger the safety of their citizens and the stability of the region, including ISIS-Khorasan (ISIS-K), al-Qa’ida (AQ), the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and its affiliates,” it said, emphasizing that their counterterrorism collaboration was “to keep both of their nations safe and secure, and as part of an enduring vision of regional peace, prosperity, and stability.” The institutionalization of this annual bilateral mechanism demonstrates that counterterrorism continues to serve as a crucial pillar of Pakistan-U.S. relations, which has long survived broader geopolitical shifts. Since the dialogue’s inauguration in 2023, the platform has steadily evolved into a structured security partnership. Pre-2023, bilateral security and counterterrorism exchanges were routinely subsumed under broader umbrella frameworks, such as the U.S.-Pakistan Strategic Dialogue or various Defense Consultative Group sessions. On these forums, counterterrorism imperatives often competed with larger and at times competing agendas. At the inaugural session of this dialogue in 2023, its primary function was to re-establish structured and formal engagement amid the post-2021 regional posture shift triggered by the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Afghanistan. The U.S.

articles.title: Myanmar Nationals Face Deportation From US After Court Ruling
articles.excerpt: A U.S. federal judge has cleared the way for President Donald Trump’s administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for nearly 4,000 people from Myanmar, presaging their possible arrest and deportation. In a ruling on Friday, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly of the Northern District of Illinois rejected last-minute efforts by immigrant rights advocates to maintain the TPS designations. The ruling came just hours after a federal judge in Boston handed down a similar ruling rejecting a challenge from an immigrant-advocacy organization against the removal of TPS status from around 232 South Sudanese nationals. Both rulings referenced a U.S. Supreme Court decision from June, which ruled that the administration had the authority to end similar protections for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. The Supreme Court ruling limited lower courts’ ability to block DHS’ efforts to end TPS for people from roughly a dozen countries, arguing that federal judges had no authority to weigh in on a challenge to TPS terminations. TPS was created by the U.S. Congress in 1990, and protects non-U.S. citizens from deportation to countries facing armed conflict or other crises posing a threat to their safety. It also grants them authorization to work in the U.S. The TPS designation for Myanmar was granted for the first time after the 2021 military coup, which was followed by a nationwide uprising against military rule. The ongoing civil war and military repression have wrecked Myanmar’s economy, displaced more than 3.5 million people, and pushed tens of thousands more to flee the country. There are around 4,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the U.S. under the TPS program.

articles.title: The Quiet Vietnamese
articles.excerpt: Vietnamese investment in Laos didn’t just grow in the first half of 2026. It nearly quadrupled. Vietnam’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs put first-quarter investment at $582 million, up 4.2 times year-on-year, with cumulative Vietnamese investment reaching $6.6 billion across 289 projects. Lao officials, speaking at July’s VIETLAO Expo in Vientiane, gave a slightly higher H1 figure of nearly $600 million, but still a 4.2-fold jump, mostly in mining, electricity, energy, and agriculture. An earlier count from March, reported by the Asia News Network, put cumulative Vietnamese state-enterprise investment at $6.21 billion across 276 projects. It confirmed Laos as Vietnam’s top outbound destination among 85 countries. VietnamNet reported Vietnam-Laos trade turnover of $1.07 billion in the first five months of 2026 (Vietnam exporting $293 million, importing $782 million), with both governments, according to the Voice of Vietnam’s coverage of the Expo, targeting $4 billion in bilateral trade for 2026 on the way to a stated goal of $10 billion by 2030. Official discussion of this topic is typically framed in terms of “great friendship,” “special solidarity,” and “strategic cohesion.” Some version of these mantras has been circulating between Vietnamese and Lao officials since the mid-1970s, and nothing in recent statements from Hanoi or Vientiane signifies an imminent break in convention. But the timing of this particular surge in investment is interesting, and reading it purely as fraternal solidarity between neighbors is naïve. The reality is that Laos is in a debt crisis, and it knows it. The small land-locked country’s trying carefully, and on its own terms, to reduce how much of its economic future drifts into the hands of Beijing. Start with the numbers that don’t get quoted in the friendship-society press releases.

articles.title: Myanmar Rejects ASEAN Call for Suu Kyi’s Release, Questions Need For Special Envoy
articles.excerpt: Myanmar’s military-backed government has again rejected the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s call for the release of detained leader Aung San Suu Kyi and dismissed the need for an ASEAN special envoy on Myanmar. The statement came on Saturday, after the 11-nation Southeast Asian bloc renewed its call for the “unconditional release” of the 81-year-old leader, who was removed from power in the February 2021 coup and remains under house arrest in Naypyidaw. On August 3, Aung San Suu Kyi was permitted to meet with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and the military authorities released four photos of the meeting. In an ASEAN Chair’s Statement dated August 7, ASEAN welcomed the meeting, describing it as “a positive step towards inclusive national dialogue and reconciliation,” but urged greater access to political detainees and reiterated its call for Suu Kyi’s “complete and unconditional release.” It also renewed its earlier request that current special envoy on Myanmar, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, be allowed to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi on her next mission to the country. In a statement on Saturday, Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected the ASEAN Chair’s request, echoing the denial that it made to an earlier request from Lazaro in late June. “Although the government has commuted her sentences based on humanitarian considerations, the matter of a full and unconditional release shall only be carried out in accordance with the law,” it said. After being removed in the coup in February 2021, Aung San Suu Kyi was charged with a range of far-fetched charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act. Despite being granted several sentence reductions, she still has more than 18 years to serve in prison.

articles.title: The Murder of a Uyghur in America Spotlights the Dangers for the Diaspora
articles.excerpt: At 10:15 p.m. on July 29, Shukur Aikebaer was abducted and murdered outside his residence in Chino County, California, by two individuals, reportedly named Zhengfeng Bo and Jianquan Bo. Aikebaer’s death sent shock waves through Uyghur communities worldwide. Investigators have not established a motive or released details about the suspects; Zhengfeng Bo was killed by police during the kidnapping. However, the incident mirrors a similar case from Uzbekistan. In July 2024, Ablehet Qahar, an Uyghur historian, was murdered in his Tashkent apartment. The crime was quietly swept under the rug, and shortly after, Qahar’s residence was barricaded and the entirety of his Uyghur historical collections disappeared. Together, the two deaths underscore a reality many Uyghurs know well: that physical distance from Xinjiang – called East Turkestan by many of the region’s native Uyghur people – no longer guarantees their safety. Over the past decade, the People’s Republic of China has dramatically expanded its efforts to stifle the voices of Uyghurs outside its borders. Reports of surveillance, harassment, threats to family, and attempted deportations have become familiar features of diaspora life. Collectively, such practices are understood as transnational repression – the effort by governments to monitor and coerce individuals living outside their territorial jurisdiction. But focusing only on Beijing’s direct actions misses a larger shift that is unfolding globally, notably in Central Asia. Most discussions of transnational repression emphasize the sending state’s own actions, whether these be intelligence services, diplomatic pressure, cyber surveillance, or direct intimidation. However, China’s growing political and economic influence appears to be producing a different dynamic, one in which repression is carried out also through the institutions of partner governments. It is, in effect, a form of transnational repression by proxy.

articles.title: The Iran-US War a Win for China? Not So Fast.
articles.excerpt: Following the outbreak of the Iran-U.S. conflict on February 28, a prevailing view emerged in international discourse that China was the primary beneficiary of the crisis. This perception was reinforced after Washington and Tehran formally signed a ceasefire agreement and launched follow-on negotiations, prompting many observers to conclude that the United States had suffered a major strategic setback while China had secured significant diplomatic, economic, and geopolitical gains. However, a broader assessment of the evolving realities facing the United States, China, Iran, and the wider Middle East suggests that the situation cannot be simply characterized as a case of American failure and Chinese success. On the contrary, as the regional order enters a new phase of adjustment, China may confront a growing number of challenges, while the United States may discover new strategic opportunities. The conflict undoubtedly imposed costs on the United States’ international image and diplomatic credibility. Despite committing substantial resources to the confrontation, Washington failed to achieve its primary strategic objectives. As the war continued, key U.S. partners in the Middle East, including Israel and several Gulf Arab states, remained exposed to Iranian military pressure and security threats, increasing the overall strategic burden on the United States. Following the cessation of hostilities, Washington faced mounting pressure from different partners. On one hand, policy differences between the United States and Israel widened considerably, with Israel urging the U.S. to maintain or even intensify pressure on Iran. On the other hand, some Gulf Arab states became increasingly dissatisfied with the U.S. inability to provide effective security guarantees and began reassessing the U.S.-centered regional security architecture that had emerged after the Cold War.

articles.title: China’s Asian Affairs Reshuffle
articles.excerpt: On July 21, President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa awarded Shen Minjuan, China’s ambassador to the country since 2023, Mongolia’s Order of the Polar Star (Altangadas), the country’s highest state honor for foreign nationals. Barely a week later, on July 29, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) updated its official organizational roster: Shen had taken office as director-general of the Department of Asian Affairs, succeeding Liu Jinsong. The speed of the promotion was striking. So was its symbolism. For Mongolian policymakers and analysts who observed Shen’s nearly three-year tenure up close, her elevation to one of the most influential operational posts in Chinese foreign policy is more than a routine bureaucratic rotation. It is the clearest signal yet that Beijing is recalibrating its approach to its immediate periphery – moving away from the overtly assertive style that defined much of the past half-decade toward a more calibrated, geoeconomics-driven model. From a Mongolian vantage point, this adjustment makes eminent strategic sense for China. Years of so-called “wolf warrior diplomacy” have yielded diminishing returns across its neighborhood. A more unyielding diplomatic approach accelerated hedging behavior in Southeast Asia, deepened security coordination between Washington and its regional allies, and made it harder for smaller states to maintain the balanced, pragmatic relations most prefer. Shen’s record in Ulaanbaatar suggests she understands this dynamic. Her task now is to apply lessons learned in a relatively manageable bilateral setting to a vastly more complex regional portfolio. The vacancy she leaves behind in Mongolia – and who fills it – will offer an early clue as to how broadly this new approach is intended to apply. This recalibration has precedents.

articles.title: Hopes for the North Korean Human Rights Act of 2026
articles.excerpt: Since the COVID-19 border closures sealed North Korea off from the world, and as the China-Russia-North Korea axis has deepened, the North Korean people have become more isolated and vulnerable than at any point in recent memory. In this grim period, one piece of encouraging news stands out: last month, U.S. Senators Tim Kaine (D-VA) and Dan Sullivan (R-AK) introduced the bipartisan North Korean Human Rights Reauthorization Act (NKHRA). Growing up in North Korea, America was my enemy – alongside South Korea, the U.S. is one of the two principal adversaries the state taught us to despise. I was taught that American missionaries had pressed the word “thief” into an innocent boy’s forehead with caustic acid. We called Americans “wolf-like Yankee imperialists” and were told they sought to swallow the Korean peninsula whole. When I escaped in 2013, I carried that conditioning with me – until American volunteers with no family ties to North Korea, no personal stake, no obligation, wept and prayed alongside me for the family I had left behind. And as I slowly learned the truth about the outside world, I discovered something that humbled me entirely: the very government I had been raised to fear had passed the North Korean Human Rights Act in 2004, becoming the first country in the world to formally recognize that what was happening inside North Korea was not merely a political problem, but ongoing crimes against humanity. The Americans had been fighting for people they would never meet, in a country they were prohibited from entering, for decades. The North Korean Human Rights Act, or NKHRA, expired in 2022. On June 25, Senators Kane and Sullivan reintroduced the NKHRA, signaling Congress’s continued commitment to advancing the rights of the North Korean people. This effort to revive the NKHRA legislation is part of a long bipartisan tradition.

articles.title: India’s Climate Stress and the Solar Power Paradox
articles.excerpt: In April and May 2026, all of the 50 hottest cities in the world were located in India, an ominous distinction for the country, which is witnessing deep, systemic climate stress. This trend has continued unabated into subsequent months, with high temperatures and humidity levels driving increased use of cooling appliances such as air conditioners across many states in India. In July 2026, India’s electrical energy consumption grew 10.93 percent year-on-year to 170.70 billion units (BU). In comparison, the country’s total power consumption was 153.88 BU in July 2025. The peak power demand also jumped to 270.20 GW in July 2026. It was 220.74 GW in July 2025. The all-time record high was set in May this year with demand of 270.82 GW. The steep rise in temperature and heat waves may be a problem for people, but for the leading air conditioner manufacturers, it is a buoyant market. Companies like Voltas and LG Electronics have reported high sales. Each had already sold over 1 million units in the first three months of the year. Panasonic India said its residential AC sales increased by 50 percent year-on-year in the summer season of 2026, representing its highest-ever level. These are very high figures for a developing country, where 60 percent of the population depends on food subsidies and power bills are on a constant rise. It also demonstrates the fact that the rising middle class, not just in metros, but also in tier-two towns and beyond, is responding to the threat and discomfort of a warming climate with significant uptake of household cooling options. Access to air conditioning, seen increasingly as a significant health issue globally, also contributes to the global warming and climate crisis. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6 percent in 2026 and 3.8 percent in 2027, driven by industry, cooling, electric vehicles (EVs), and data centers.

Du Centre-Val de Loire à la Nouvelle-Aquitaine, elles seront comprises entre 38 °C et 40 °C. En Ile-de-France elles seront voisines de 38 °C. » Il ne s’agit pas d’une « nouvelle » canicule à proprement parler, précisait déjà mardi le prévisionniste, mais plutôt de la suite de la troisième vague de chaleur qui a commencé le 28 juillet et ne s’est toujours pas arrêtée, au moins dans le Sud-Est.
articles.summary: 周三，法国气象局将78个省份列为高温橙色警戒，而周二这一数字为43个。这轮新的高温天气预计将持续数日。周二，科西嘉岛的气温超过了40摄氏度，其中萨尔特内最高达到40.6摄氏度。其他地区也录得高温：茹埃莱图尔和沙托梅扬为39摄氏度，丰特奈、伊苏丹、普雷姆里、桑特和尼姆为38摄氏度，其中尼姆比季节正常值高7摄氏度。多个大城市气温也显著高于均值：南特37摄氏度（比正常高12度），雷恩36摄氏度（高11度），图尔36摄氏度（高10度），里昂35摄氏度（高7度），巴黎33摄氏度（高8度）。波尔多达到37摄氏度，比季节正常值高9度。法国气象局预计周四大部分地区最高气温将超过35摄氏度，中央-卢瓦尔河谷至新阿基坦地区在38至40摄氏度之间，巴黎大区接近38摄氏度。这并非新一轮“热浪”，而是自7月28日开始的第三轮热浪的延续，至少在东南部尚未结束。

articles.title: SED-Opferbeauftragte will DDR-Geschichte im Unterricht verankern
articles.excerpt: Damit das Unrecht der DDR nicht in Vergessenheit gerät, fordert die SED-Opferbeauftragte des Bundestags, Evelyn Zupke, eine feste Verankerung im Schulunterricht. »DDR-Geschichte wird oft nicht verbindlich genug in der Schule behandelt. Das ist ein Problem«, sagte sie der »Rheinischen Post« einen Tag vor dem 65. Jahrestag des Mauerbaus. »Ich würde mir wünschen, dass jede Schülerin und jeder Schüler wenigstens einmal eine Gedenkstätte zur zweiten deutschen Diktatur besucht.«Trotz des föderalen Bildungssystems müssten Wege gefunden werden, das Thema sowohl im Osten als auch im Westen besser abzusichern. Die Schüler müssten in Bezug auf die DDR das Verständnis entwickeln, »dass es sich um eine Diktatur und einen Unrechtsstaat gehandelt hat«, mahnte Zupke.Sie sei besorgt, die SED-Diktatur könne zu »einer bloßen Fußnote der Geschichte« werden, »gerade in einer Zeit, in der die Generation der Zeitzeugen immer kleiner wird«. Wie Zupke dem »Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland« mitteilte, beziehen noch rund 37.000 Menschen die sogenannte Opferrente. Anspruch auf die monatliche Leistung haben jene, die in der DDR mehr als 90 Tage lang aus politischen Gründen inhaftiert waren. Erinnerung durch StraßennamenMit Blick auf den 65. Jahrestag des Baus der Berliner Mauer mahnte Zupke: »Das Unrecht an der Berliner Mauer und der innerdeutschen Grenze zeigt uns überdeutlich, dass die DDR eine Diktatur war. Wer die DDR heute verklärt, handelt nicht nur geschichtsvergessen. Es ist zugleich auch ein Schlag ins Gesicht Tausender Opfer politischer Gewalt in der DDR.«Zupke verwies zugleich auf das Ausmaß politischer Verfolgung: Zwischen 1945 und 1989 habe es etwa 250.000 politische Häftlinge in den Haftanstalten und Jugendwerkhöfen gegeben, zudem weitere Opfergruppen wie Zwangsausgesiedelte und Menschen, die »von den staatlichen Institutionen systematisch psychisch zersetzt wurden«.

articles.title: Spanien: Flüchtlingspolitik in der Kritik - Giorgia Meloni und Mette Frederiksen in Flüchtlingsfrage vereint
articles.excerpt: Schwedens liberalkonservativer Premierminister geht Spaniens linke Regierung hart an. Der Grund? Die Entscheidung, Menschen ohne Aufenthaltspapiere eine Amnestie zu gewähren. Ulf Kristersson, der seine Heimat gestützt von Rechtspopulisten regiert , bezeichnet das im Gespräch mit der »Financial Times« als eine »sehe schlechte Idee«. Seine Äußerungen fallen in eine Woche, in der bereits zwei weitere EU-Ministerpräsidentinnen die Debatte über das Thema Migration forciert haben. Die Ministerpräsidentinnen von Italien und Dänemark, Giorgia Meloni und Mette Frederiksen, haben in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung vor »unkontrollierter Migration« nach Europa gewarnt. Beide sprachen sich erneut für sogenannte Rückführungszentren außerhalb der EU aus, um abgelehnte Asylbewerber in ihre Heimatländer zurückzubringen. In der Erklärung, die über soziale Netzwerke verbreitet wurde, heißt es: »Wir akzeptieren keine unkontrollierte Migration nach Europa.« Ungeachtet politischer Unterschiede sei man verbunden durch den Wunsch nach einem Schutz Europas und seiner Werte. Durch illegale Einwanderung stiegen die Kriminalitätsraten, öffentliche Dienstleistungen würden zunehmend belastet und Bürger verlören Vertrauen. Folge seien negative Auswirkungen auf die europäischen Gesellschaften. Als besonders schwerwiegend bezeichneten es Meloni und Frederiksen, »wenn illegale Migranten, die kein Aufenthaltsrecht in unseren Ländern haben, Gewaltverbrechen begehen, mit Drogen handeln oder sich sexueller Gewaltschuldig machen«. Auf Anweisung von Meloni hatte Italien nach dem Ansturm von mehr als 70.000 Migranten auf die spanische Exklave Ceuta Anfang des Monats wieder Grenzkontrollen zu Spanien eingeführt. Die linke Regierung in Madrid lässt seit dem Wochenende Reisende aus Italien wieder kontrollieren.Die Zahl der irregulären Grenzübertritte in die EU ist in den vergangenen Jahren deutlich zurückgegangen.

articles.title: Catering-Wagen statt »Air Force One«? Trump bestätigt Ablenkungsmanöver des Secret Service
articles.excerpt: Das Täuschungsmanöver auf dem Rückflug von US-Präsident Donald Trump aus der Türkei ist seinen Angaben zufolge auf Weisung seiner Personenschützer erfolgt. Er richte sich nach deren Vorgaben, sagte der Republikaner auf Nachfragen von Reportern. »Das liegt allein beim Secret Service.« Das gelte auch für das Militär. »Ich tue, was sie sagen.« Der Secret Service ist unter anderem für die Sicherheit des Präsidenten zuständig.Zum Hintergrund der Entscheidung machte Trump keine genauen Angaben. Er sagte: »Ich nehme an, dass es eine Bedrohung gab.« Er habe nicht weiter nachgefragt. Zugleich schien der Präsident bemüht, dem Fall keine große Bedeutung beizumessen: »Ich bekomme viele Drohungen.« Er ergänzte: »Jeder Präsident, der etwas bewirkt, ist mit zahlreichen Drohungen konfrontiert. Präsidenten, die nichts bewirken, bekommen keine Drohungen.«Die »Washington Post« hatte am Montag (Ortszeit) enthüllt, dass das Weiße Haus im Juli nach dem Nato-Gipfel nur vorgetäuscht hatte, dass Trump mit einer Regierungsmaschine aus Ankara abgeflogen war. Der 80-Jährige stieg dort vor laufenden Kameras in die Regierungsmaschine ein, stieg dann aber laut der Zeitung unbemerkt in einen seitlich an dem Jet platzierten Catering-Container. Dessen Laster brachte ihn auf dem Flughafen inkognito zu einem kleineren US-Militärflugzeug, mit dem er nach Großbritannien flog. Nach der Landung der Regierungsmaschine in Großbritannien wechselte der Tross des Präsidenten von der alten, hellblauen Boeing 747 in den neuen Jet, der Trump von Katar geschenkt worden war. Der Präsident stieg dort auch in die »Air Force One« um. Die Öffentlichkeit sollte den Eindruck bekommen, dass er die ganze Reise in den Regierungsmaschinen zurückgelegt habe. In den USA stieg er dann vor laufenden Kameras aus.
articles.summary: 美国总统唐纳德·特朗普表示，他在从土耳其返程途中的伪装行动是遵照其保镖的指示进行的。这位共和党人在回应记者提问时说：“我听从他们的安排。这完全取决于特勤局。”这也适用于军方，他说：“他们怎么说，我就怎么做。”特勤局负责总统的安全。特朗普没有透露决定背后的具体原因，仅表示：“我猜想存在威胁。”他并未进一步追问。同时，他似乎淡化此事的重要性：“我收到过很多威胁。”他补充说：“每一位有所作为的总统都面临无数威胁；无所作为的总统则不会。”据《华盛顿邮报》周一报道，白宫在7月北约峰会后曾假装特朗普从安卡拉乘坐政府飞机离开。这位80岁的总统在镜头前登上政府飞机，但随后悄悄进入停在飞机旁的餐饮集装箱，由卡车将他匿名送往机场内一架较小的美军飞机，飞往英国。政府飞机在英国降落后，特朗普随行团队从旧的天蓝色波音747换乘卡塔尔赠送的新飞机，并在那里登上了空军一号。公众误以为他全程乘坐政府飞机。在美国，他则在镜头前走下飞机。

articles.title: Autofarben »Cement« und »Graphite«: Müssen Deutschlands Straßen echt noch grauer werden?
News: Friedrich Merz, Lars Klingbeil, BND, Mohsen Rezaee, Donald Trump, Sonnenfinsternis
articles.excerpt: Lizenz zur AttackeEs ist wohl mit Glück zu erklären, dass die mit Sprengstoff ausgerüstete Drohne am 4. August auf dem Flughafen Leipzig/Halle nicht explodierte. Ihr Ziel war offenbar eine ukrainische Antonow An-124; der Zünder war wohl defekt. Seither ermittelt die Bundesanwaltschaft, der Nationale Sicherheitsrat tagte. Ukrainische Antonow auf dem Flughafen Leipzig/Halle Foto: Hendrik Schmidt / dpa Während das »Wall Street Journal« am 7. August unter Berufung auf zwei amerikanische Beamte meldete, US-Dienste machten für die Leipziger Drohne die russische Regierung verantwortlich, spricht Innenminister Alexander Dobrindt seit einer Woche von einem »hybriden Anschlagsszenario« und »fremden Mächten« (mehr hier ). Noch ist also nicht bewiesen, dass Russland hinter dem Angriff steckt. Klar ist aber: Deutschland ist längst Ziel hybrider Kriegsführung. Heute um 10 Uhr beschließt das Kabinett eine Reform der deutschen Nachrichtendienste, nicht wegen Leipzig, aber unter dem Eindruck der Ereignisse von Leipzig. Und auch hier kann man durchaus von einer Zeitenwende sprechen. Bundesnachrichtendienst und Verfassungsschutz sollen deutlich mehr Befugnisse erhalten (mehr dazu hier ). Der BND soll nicht mehr nur Informationen sammeln, sondern in begrenzten Fällen aktiv eingreifen dürfen. Er könnte ausländische IT-Systeme hacken, die Infrastruktur gegnerischer Cyberangriffe lahmlegen und in einer »nachrichtendienstlichen Sonderlage« sogar die Angriffsfähigkeit eines Gegners schwächen. Denkbar wäre auch eine Sabotageaktion gegen eine russische Drohnenfabrik. BND-Präsident Martin Jäger sagt, man müsse dem Gegner zeigen, »dass wir in der Lage sind, sehr ähnliche Dinge zu tun, damit auch die andere Seite den Schmerz spürt«.Neu erlaubt werden auch die Online-Durchsuchung und der Abgleich von biometrischen Daten mit Ergebnissen aus dem Internet. Zugleich sollen die Dienste auch besser kontrolliert werden.

articles.title: Nordkorea feuert erneut ballistische Rakete ab – Anrainer warnen vor Risiken unangekündigter Tests

Nach Angaben des japanischen Verteidigungsministeriums erreichte der Flugkörper eine maximale Höhe von rund 90 Kilometern und eine Reichweite von knapp 700 Kilometern, ehe er im Meer aufprallte. Wie Südkoreas amtliche Nachrichtenagentur Yonhap berichtete, war das Geschoss am Himmel für einige Anwohner Südkoreas in der nordöstlichen Küstenregion mit bloßem Auge sichtbar. August beginnen. Dem abgeschotteten Land unter Führung von Machthaber Kim Jong Un ist es gemäß mehreren Resolutionen des Uno-Sicherheitsrats grundsätzlich untersagt, ballistische Raketen abzufeuern. articles.title: Österreich: Wanderer aus Deutschland in Tiroler Bergen tödlich verunglückt
articles.excerpt: Ein Wanderer aus Nordrhein-Westfalen ist nach einer dramatischen Suchaktion in den Tiroler Bergen in Österreich tot aufgefunden worden. Der 74-Jährige aus dem Landkreis Olpe sei vermutlich über nahezu senkrechte Felswände abgestürzt, wie die Polizei mitteilte . Behalten Sie den Überblick: Jeden Werktag gegen 18 Uhr beantworten SPIEGEL-Autorinnen und -Autoren die wichtigsten Fragen des Tages im Newsletter »Die Lage am Abend« – hintergründig, kompakt, kostenlos. Er kehrte allerdings nicht zurück. Der Betreiber seiner Unterkunft meldete ihn gegen 20.50 Uhr als vermisst. Suche mit Hubschrauber, Drohne und HundenZunächst suchte die Polizei am Montagabend mit einem Hubschrauber und einer Drohne nach dem Vermissten. In der Dunkelheit machten sich auch Mannschaften der Bergrettung mit fünf Suchhunden über verschiedene Routen auf den Weg, um den Mann zu finden. Bei starkem Wind und Regen erreichten sie nach Mitternacht ein knapp 2800 Meter hohes Bergjoch, wo sie den Wanderer vermuteten. Doch die Suche blieb vorerst erfolglos. Am Dienstagmorgen startete der Polizeihubschrauber erneut einen Suchflug. Nach etwa einer Stunde wurde eine leblose Person im Bereich eines Gebirgsbaches auf knapp 2300 Metern Seehöhe gefunden.Die Polizei geht nach eigenen Angaben davon aus, dass der Wanderer beim Abstieg von dem Bergjoch den markierten Pfad verlassen hatte. Er dürfte dann durch immer steileres Gelände abgestiegen »und anschließend über nahezu senkrechte Wände abgestürzt sein«, hieß es. Der tödliche Ausgang einer Tour am Großglockner bewegte viele Menschen. Die Alpinkletterer Babsi Zangerl und Jacopo Larcher erklären, wie sie als Paar am Berg funktionieren.
